title: Karate for kids
metaDescription: What happens in a children's Kyokushin class, what protective gear is used, and how children are kept safe.

text.text: What actually happens in a children's class, what it costs, and how we keep them safe.
Kyokushin is full-contact karate. That worries parents, and it should — so here is exactly how it works for children.
Most dojo take children from around six. Some take younger. Ask your local sensei, because it depends on the class mix on the night.

Not in the first months, and not before they are ready. Beginners spend their time on stances, blocks, kicks in the air and how the class works. Contact is introduced gradually, supervised, and matched to age and grade.
Children never spar adults.
At tournaments, protective equipment is compulsory. Nobody competes without it.
Every competitor
Under 18s, additionally
Under 10s, additionally
Your sensei will tell you what to buy and where. You don't need any of it to start training — only to compete.

blocks.text: Fitness — and how we build it

text.text: We work on a child's physical condition from the start. The first standard we build towards is twenty press-ups, twenty sit-ups and twenty squats or belt jumps.

Nobody is expected to manage that on their first night. Some children arrive able to do two press-ups, and that is fine — we start where they are and add to it. What we don't do is pretend the standard isn't there.

blocks.text: Discipline, and why it's the point

text.text: This is budo karate. Budo means the martial way, and it puts character ahead of technique. Children bow when they enter the dojo, line up when they're told to, and listen when someone is speaking. That is not incidental to the training — it is most of the training.
If you're hoping karate will help your child with focus, self-control or confidence, that is exactly what this part does.

None of which means the classes are grim. They're not. We make it fun, because a child who isn't enjoying themselves doesn't come back — and because the discipline works better when it's wrapped around something they want to do.
Yes. Parents are welcome to stay for any class, at any dojo, at any time. You never need to ask.
Each dojo sets its own fees, so check your local dojo's page. Your child's first class is free everywhere, and you don't need a gi for the first few weeks — shorts and a t-shirt is fine.
Yes. There is no term to wait for and no intake date. Turn up on a training night and start.

blocks.text: What do they get out of it?

text.text: A grading every few months, so progress is visible. A belt they earned rather than were given. Training alongside adults and older students, which children take more seriously than they let on.
And a road that goes a long way — national gradings, tournaments, camps, and eventually a black belt.

title: The belt system explained
metaDescription: What the belt colours mean, how long each grade takes, and what a grading involves.

text.text: What the colours mean, how long each takes, and why nobody in the dojo makes much of them.
Belts are a progress marker, not a ranking of worth. They exist so a student can see how far they have come and an instructor can see what to teach next.
Grades below black belt are
kyu
grades, and they count downwards — 10th kyu is a beginner, 1st kyu is the grade immediately before black belt. Grades from black belt upwards are
dan
grades, and they count upwards.
So a student goes 10th kyu, 9th, 8th and so on down to 1st kyu, then shodan — first dan, black belt — and then counts up again.
Early grades come quickly — often a few months apart — because early progress is fast and visible. The gaps widen as you go up. The step from 1st kyu to shodan is measured in years, not months.
Nobody is graded on time served. You grade when your instructor judges you ready, and the grading itself is the test.

Kihon — the basic techniques. Kata — the set forms. Kumite — sparring, appropriate to your age and grade. Fitness. And, from a certain point, the ability to keep going when you are tired, which is much of what is being examined.
Junior gradings are scaled to the child. A seven-year-old is not doing what an adult brown belt is doing.

It is the oldest line in karate and it is still true. Shodan means a student has the basics in order and can now start learning properly. Above it the dan grades continue — and in MOKNZ they continue to eighth.
Which is the honest answer to how long a black belt takes: several years to reach, and then the rest of your life.

title: The dojo oath
metaDescription: The seven lines of the Kyokushin dojo kun, what they mean, and where they came from.

text.text: Seven lines, spoken at the end of every session, in every MOKNZ dojo. Here is what they mean and where they came from.
At the close of training the senior instructor speaks each line and the class repeats it. It takes under a minute. It has ended Kyokushin training sessions since the first honbu dojo opened in Tokyo.
Every line begins with
hitotsu
— "one". Not first, second, third. Each is equally the first, and none outranks another.
The instructor speaks each line; the class repeats it.
Hitotsu, ware ware wa, shinshin o renmashi kakko fubatsu no shingi o kiwameru koto.
We will train our hearts and bodies for a firm unshaking spirit.
Hitotsu, ware ware wa, bu no shinzui o kiwame, ki ni hasshi, kan ni bin naru koto.
We will pursue the true meaning of the martial way so that in time our senses may be alert.
Hitotsu, ware ware wa, shitsujitsu goken o mot-te, jiko no seishin o kanyo suru koto.
With true vigor, we will seek to cultivate a spirit of self denial.
Hitotsu, ware ware wa, reisetsu o omonji, chojo o keishi, sobo no furumai o tsutsushimu koto.
We will respect our superiors and refrain from violence.
Hitotsu, ware ware wa, shinbutsu o totobi, kenjo no bitoku o wasurezaru koto.
We will follow and honour our conscience and never forget the true virtue of humility.
Hitotsu, ware ware wa, chisei to tairyoku to o kojo sase, koto ni nozonde ayamatazaru koto.
We will look up to wisdom and strength, not seeking other desires.
Hitotsu, ware ware wa, shogai no shugyo o karate no michi ni tsuji, Kyokushin no michi o matto suru koto.
All our lives, through the discipline of karate, we will seek to fulfill the true meaning of the Kyokushin way.
Recited at the end of every session, in Japanese or English depending on the dojo.

blocks.text: What the seven lines ask of you

text.text: The wording is plain enough that it barely needs explaining, but it repays a little thought — particularly for a new student wondering what they have just agreed to.

blocks.text: Train the heart as well as the body

text.text: The first line puts them together deliberately. A strong body with no character behind it is not the point of any of this.

blocks.text: Pursue what the martial way actually means

text.text: Not technique for its own sake. The promise is that if you keep looking, your judgement sharpens — you notice more, and sooner.
Turning up when you don't feel like it. Finishing the set. Choosing the harder option when nobody would know either way.

blocks.text: Respect your seniors, refrain from violence

text.text: The second half is the one that surprises people. A full-contact style, and the oath explicitly forbids using it. That is not a contradiction — it is the whole reason the training is safe to give anyone.

blocks.text: Follow your conscience, and stay humble

text.text: Humility is named as a virtue rather than a manner. It's what stops skill turning into arrogance, and it is why nobody in the dojo makes much of their grade.

blocks.text: Look up to wisdom and strength, and want little else

text.text: A line about what you point yourself at. Two things worth chasing, and a warning that most of the rest is noise.
The last line makes the timeframe explicit. Not until black belt. Not until you stop competing. All of it.
Not Sosai Mas Oyama. He asked someone else.
Oyama's favourite book was Eiji Yoshikawa's
Musashi

, the story of the undefeated two-sword swordsman Miyamoto Musashi. He had taken it with him into the mountains during his years of solitary training, and by the time he came down and built the honbu dojo in Tokyo, he wanted an oath for the wall — and he wanted Yoshikawa to write it.

So he began turning up outside the novelist's house with a packed lunch and waiting under a tree. He did this, by his wife's account, for something like six months, without ever knocking. Too polite to impose.

One day the back gate was open and he could see two of the household's maids splitting firewood. He went in and did it for them. When Yoshikawa later wandered into his garden and found the wood stacked neatly, he asked who was responsible, and was told about the man who had been waiting outside for half a year.

They met. Oyama explained what he wanted and admitted he had no money to pay for it. Yoshikawa's answer was that the firewood had bought him hotter baths every night for weeks, so the debt already ran the other way.

The story comes from an interview with Chiyako Oyama, Sosai's wife, who said her husband felt more strongly about the dojo kun than almost anything, and asked that students keep saying it after every session.
Retold here in our own words, from an account given by Sosai's wife. If your dojo has its own version of this story, we would like to hear it.

title: Keeping children safe
metaDescription: How children are protected in our dojo, and what to do if something worries you.

text.text: Children train in our dojo throughout New Zealand. This page sets out how we protect them and what to do if something concerns you.
Everyone who instructs or supervises children in a MOKNZ dojo is police vetted before they teach, and re-vetted regularly.
You may stay and watch any class, at any dojo, at any time. You never need to ask permission and you never need a reason.
Children are not taught behind closed doors.

items.text: Contact is introduced gradually and matched to age and grade.
Protective equipment is compulsory for tournaments — see
Instruction happens in the open, in the dojo, during class time.

text.text: If something worries you — about an instructor, another student, or anything you have seen or been told — you can raise it directly and it will be taken seriously.
You do not have to go through your dojo. If your concern is about someone at your dojo, contact the national officer directly.

blocks.text: If a child is in immediate danger

text.text: Call 111.
You can also contact Oranga Tamariki on 0508 326 459, at any hour, whether or not you have spoken to us.
You do not need our permission to report a concern to the authorities, and we will never ask you to come to us first.
We ask permission before photographing a child for the website or social media, and we will remove any photograph on request.

title: Bringing your dojo to MOKNZ
metaDescription: For instructors who run a Kyokushin dojo and are considering a change of affiliation.

text.text: If you run a Kyokushin dojo and you're considering a change of affiliation, this page is written for you rather than for prospective students.
We know what's involved. A move affects your grade, your students' grades, your syllabus and your income, and it usually can't be discussed openly until it's decided.
Your dojo sets its own fees. MOKNZ does not set them and does not take a percentage.
You keep your dojo name, your premises, your training nights and your students.
Students transferring with their dojo generally retain their current kyu grade. We are not going to put your brown belts back into white.
The syllabus is broadly common across Kyokushin. Kata, kihon and the grading structure will be familiar, and the differences are matters of detail rather than substance.

items.text: Direct lineage to Sosai Mas Oyama
Hanshi Doug Holloway, 8th dan, opened the first Kyokushin dojo in New Zealand in 1965.
With a panel that includes 7th and 8th dan.
Open to your students from the day you affiliate.
A dojo website, registration and payment collection
Set up for you. Your subs land in your account.

blocks.intro: Tell us your name, your grade, your town, roughly how many students you have, and your current affiliation. Say how best to reach you.

title: The 50 Man Kumite
metaDescription: Fifty consecutive full-contact fights, and the New Zealanders who have completed them.

text.text: Fifty consecutive full-contact fights, one after another. Nine times in our history.
A fresh opponent every two minutes, fifty times over, with no rest between fights. Most attempts do not finish.
Sosai Mas Oyama set the test as the measure of what a black belt should be able to endure. It is not a competition and there is no prize. You either finish or you do not.
In sixty years of Kyokushin in New Zealand, it has been completed nine times.
Graeme Gavegan has completed it twice, eight years apart.
Kyoshi Mike Kenworthy and Kyoshi Graeme Gavegan lead alongside Hanshi Doug Holloway. Shihan Kelvin McSkimming, Shihan Russell Dilloway and Renshi Sean O'Connell are our branch chiefs.
All six are on this board. The people running MOKNZ have done the hardest thing the style asks of anyone.

title: Start training
metaDescription: What happens on your first night, and answers to the usual questions.

text.text: Nobody walks into a dojo for the first time feeling confident. Here's exactly what happens, so you know before you arrive.

items.text: Tell whoever's at the door it's your first time. No booking needed.
You'll train barefoot. Bring water. That's the whole list.
Stances, blocks, and how we line up. Contact comes much later, and only when you're ready.

items.q: Am I too old? Too unfit?

a.text: Our dojo have people training from five to sixty-five. You work at your own pace from the first night.

We do build fitness deliberately — the first standard we work towards is twenty press-ups, twenty sit-ups and twenty squats. You are not expected to arrive able to do that. You are expected to keep turning up.
It is, eventually, and only for those who want it. Beginners spend months on basics before any contact at all.
Not for the first few weeks. Buy one once you know you're staying.
Each dojo sets its own fees, so check your local dojo's page. Your first class is free everywhere.
Yes. There is no term to wait for and no intake date. Turn up on a training night and start.
